paper_title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Modern image and video generators use diffusion or flow objectives (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023) to train scalable denoising networks (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Brooks et al., 2024) to predict target along the noising path, such as the noise ϵ, the clean data x, or the velocity := ϵx. The choice of target is central design decision: given the noisy input and timestep, these quantities carry the same information, yet they define distinct regression problems with substantially different training behavior and sample quality (Karras et al., 2022; Salimans & Ho, 2022). Existing hand-designed choices occupy small corner of much larger design space: velocity in latent models (Esser et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) or clean data in recent pixel models (Li & He, 2026; Guo et al., 2026), with methods also exploring interpolation between standard targets (Jin & Wang, 2026) or masking part of the noise component (Chen et al., 2026a). We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces this hand-designed choice with fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically. It defines the target uW := ϵ x, where is positive semidefinite (PSD) matrix that applies separate learnable nonnegative weight wi to the noise along each direction of jointly learned orthogonal basis. Up to sign and overall scale, the target family includes noise prediction at wi +, clean-data prediction at wi = 0, velocity prediction at wi = 1, shared scalar interpolations at wi w, and binary low-rank masks at wi {0, 1}. closed-form map recovers the velocity from the networks prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. AnisoFlow is particularly effective in pixel space, where patchification places many pixel coordinates within each transformer token, exposing directions with widely varying data variance (Li & He, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a) and creating setting where different directions can benefit from different prediction targets. The velocity target places unit noise weight in every direction, increasing the difficulty of prediction in low-variance directions. Clean-data prediction removes the noise component but can be harder in high-variance directions and makes velocity recovery ill-conditioned at low noise. AnisoFlow resolves this tradeoff by learning separate noise weight for each direction. We theoretically analyze which noise weights make prediction easiest for the network. We study the prediction error in the PCA basis, which diagonalizes the data covariance and closely matches the basis that AnisoFlow learns empirically. Under local frozen-error model, we derive the preferred weight in each direction and show that it scales near-linearly with data variance. Consistent with this analysis, pixel-space models learn weights that follow the scaling wi cλi, where λi is the data variance in direction i. Empirically, AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT-H/16 baseline on ImageNet 256256 in pixel space, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely eliminates patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference. In latent-space models, AnisoFlow recovers weights close to the default velocity target in SiT (Ma et al., 2024) with SD-VAE (Rombach et al., 2022) and the default clean-data target in RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026), achieving comparable performance. Our contributions include (a) AnisoFlow, fully learnable prediction-target family that subsumes standard targets as special cases; (b) theoretical analysis relating the preferred noise weights to the networks prediction errors, explaining the observed near-linear scaling and approximate timestep invariance; and (c) state-of-the-art pixel-space generation on ImageNet and improved quality and stability in text-to-image generation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Standard prediction parameterizations. The choice among noise (ϵ)-, velocity (u)-, and cleandata (x)-prediction determines how the target combines the data and noise components and can substantially affect training behavior and sample quality (Karras et al., 2022; Salimans & Ho, 2022; Jin & Wang, 2026). Noiseand velocity-prediction assign nonzero noise coefficient to every direction, which can make regression difficult in high-dimensional pixel space (Li & He, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Jin & Wang, 2026). Clean-data prediction avoids predicting the noise, but recovering

Interpolated targets. Isotropic interpolations mix data and noise with the same coefficient in every direction: EDM (Karras et al., 2022) sets this coefficient analytically through σt-dependent skip connection, and k-Diff (Jin & Wang, 2026) learns it as single scalar. AsymFlow (Chen et al., 2026a) is anisotropic but binary, combining velocity prediction in low-rank subspace and data prediction in the orthogonal complement. Both k-Diff and AsymFlow lie within AnisoFlows target family, as shared scalar and binary profile. Appendix A.2 shows that per-direction extension of EDMs choice is exactly what our analysis predicts when the network has no information beyond the timestep. Recent work also studies how prediction parameterizations interact with representation dimension, covariance conditioning, and low-variance directions (Fu et al., 2026; Gagneux et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang & Pehlevan, 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Ahamed et al., 2026). Rotation-based quantization. The rotate-then-scale form of AnisoFlows recovery resembles rotation-based quantization (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025), which applies fixed or learned orthogonal transforms to weights and activations to suppress outliers before quantization. These methods operate layer-wise on trained network, whereas AnisoFlow learns network-wide preconditioning through the prediction target, jointly with the network.

sections.title: 4 ANISOTROPIC FLOW MODELS

sections.content: We analyze how the learned weights relate to the data spectrum and why single weight profile suffices across timesteps. We study each direction of the PCA basis separately. sections.content: Experimental setup. We evaluate AnisoFlow on class-conditional ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) 256256 and text-to-image generation in pixel-space, and then further extend it to latent-space flow models. In each setting, we preserve the architecture and training recipe of the underlying model and change only the prediction-target parameterization. For our main pixel-space experiments, we use JiT-H/16 (Li & He, 2026), with JiT-B/16 for smaller-scale experiments. We report FID (Heusel et al., 2017) under the ADM evaluation protocol (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021). sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Figure 7: Latent-space weights. Learned weights in SiT-REPA and RAEv2 are close to their default targets. AnisoFlow replaces fixed prediction targets with learnable anisotropic target, assigning separate noise weight to each direction in learned basis. In pixel space, the learned basis aligns with PCA and the weights scale near-linearly with data variance, consistent with our prediction-error analysis. Empirically, AnisoFlow substantially improves FID over the JiT baseline on ImageNet without representation alignment or architectural changes, while improving image quality and numerical stability in text-to-image generation. These results show that prediction targets can adapt to the data and the models errors rather than being fixed in advance.

We initialize = and use the spectral update with EMA coefficient 105. RAEv2. We also evaluate AnisoFlow on RAEv2, preserving its representation, architecture, and Muon-based training recipe (Jordan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a). During training, the spectral basis update additionally maintains running moment matrix and eigendecomposes it at every step to update B. At each model evaluation, prediction and velocity recovery require transforms into and out of the learned basis together with elementwise directional operations. The eigendecomposition of the running moment is performed at every optimization step during training only; at inference time, the learned basis is fixed. sections.content: Effect of the input bottleneck. JiT represents each 16 16 RGB patch as 768-dimensional pixel vector, which is projected through 256-dimensional linear patch embedding before entering the transformer. Thus, only 256-dimensional projection of the original patch is directly available to the network. To test whether the learned target reflects this architectural bottleneck, we learn weights across the full 768-dimensional PCA spectrum. The learned weights follow the near-linear spectral profile of the main experiments through roughly the patch-embedding dimension, but change noticeably beyond this point  (Fig. 9)  . The transition near dimension 256 suggests that the learned target is sensitive to the networks input bottleneck. The zero-skill limit of Appendix A.2 provides limiting case in which directional information is entirely unavailable. Figure 9: Effect of the JiT input bottleneck. Untrimmed version of Fig. 3a, showing all 768 directional variance/weight pairs for the frozen PCA basis and learnable bases with and without PCA initialization. Both learnable variants use spectral updates; the dashed line shows = 0.15λ. The near-linear profile at high variance changes noticeably in the low-variance directions beyond roughly the 256-dimensional patch-embedding bottleneck. Cross-direction coupling. Although our theory analyzes each direction separately, the shared network can couple the preferred weights across directions. Using JiT-B/16 with fixed PCA basis, we select 32 directions whose weights remain learnable and freeze all other directional weights to fixed background profile. As shown in Fig. 10, for the highest-variance directions, the free weights remain close to the fully learned solution under both frozen backgrounds, whereas lower-variance directions exhibit somewhat greater sensitivity to the complementary targets. These results support the direction-wise approximation used in our analysis while indicating mild cross-direction coupling in the lowest-variance directions.
